claim: Single bacterial cells have been found to grow predominantly exponentially.
source: So far, single bacterial cells have been found to grow predominantly exponentially, which implies the need for tight regulation to maintain cell size homeostasis.
evidence: This is a general statement about bacterial growth supported by citations in the introduction section.

claim: C. glutamicum exhibits asymptotically linear single-cell growth.
source: Here, we characterize the growth behavior of the apically growing bacterium Corynebacterium glutamicum using a novel broadly applicable inference method for single-cell growth dynamics. Using this approach, we find that C. glutamicum exhibits asymptotically linear single-cell growth.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by experimental data and analysis presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The distribution of cell lengths is narrower for linear than exponential growth.
source: Finally, with simulations we show that the distribution of cell lengths is narrower for linear than exponential growth, suggesting that this asymptotically linear growth mode can act as a substitute for tight division length and division symmetry regulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Exponential growth implies the need for tight regulation to maintain cell size homeostasis.
source: So far, single bacterial cells have been found to grow predominantly exponentially, which implies the need for tight regulation to maintain cell size homeostasis.
evidence: This is a theoretical inference about the implications of exponential growth.

claim: E. coli, B. subtilis, and C. crescentus grow exponentially at the single-cell level when averaged over the cell cycle.
source: Extensive work was done on common model organisms, including Escherichia coli, Bacillus subtilis, and Caulobacter crescentus, revealing that averaged over the cell cycle, single cells grow exponentially for these species (Taheri-Araghi et al., 2015; Mir et al., 2011; Iyer-Biswas et al., 2014; Yu et al., 2017; Godin et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Single-cell exponential growth is expected if cellular volume production is proportional to the protein content.
source: Single-cell exponential growth is expected if cellular volume production is proportional to the protein content (Amir, 2014), as shown to be the case for E. coli (Belliveau et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical and experimental work.

claim: For E. coli, cellular volume production is proportional to protein content.
source: Single-cell exponential growth is expected if cellular volume production is proportional to the protein content (Amir, 2014), as shown to be the case for E. coli (Belliveau et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to experimental work on E. coli.

claim: B. subtilis exhibits biphasic growth with a phase of approximately constant elongation rate followed by a phase of increasing elongation rate.
source: For B. subtilis (Nordholt et al., 2020), a biphasic growth mode was observed, where a phase of approximately constant elongation rate is followed by a phase of increasing elongation rate.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work on B. subtilis.

claim: E. coli shows evidence for super-exponential growth in the later stages of the cell cycle.
source: For E. coli, a new method provides evidence for super-exponential in the later stages of the cell cycle (Kar et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to recent work on E. coli.

claim: C. glutamicum is a rod-shaped bacterium that grows its cell wall exclusively at the cell poles.
source: This rod-shaped bacterium grows its cell wall exclusively at the cell poles, allowing, in principle, for deviations from exponential single-cell growth (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a known characteristic of C. glutamicum supported by established knowledge and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Exponential growth requires checkpoints and regulatory systems to maintain a constant size distribution.
source: while exponential growth requires checkpoints and regulatory systems to maintain a constant size distribution (Mir et al., 2011), such tight regulation might not be needed for other growth modes.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous theoretical work.

claim: C. glutamicum is broadly used as a production-organism for amino-acids and vitamins.
source: Corynebacterium glutamicum is broadly used as a production-organism for amino-acids and vitamins and also serves as model organism for the taxonomically related human pathogens Corynebacterium diphteriae and Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Hermann, 2003; Antoine et al., 1988; Schubert et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge about C. glutamicum supported by citations.

claim: C. glutamicum serves as a model organism for C. diphteriae and M. tuberculosis.
source: Corynebacterium glutamicum is broadly used as a production-organism for amino-acids and vitamins and also serves as model organism for the taxonomically related human pathogens Corynebacterium diphteriae and Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Hermann, 2003; Antoine et al., 1988; Schubert et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The cell wall of Corynebacteria and Mycobacteria is composed of a peptidoglycan sacculus covalently bound to an arabinogalactan layer.
source: The cell wall of these bacteria is a polymer assembly composed of a classical bacterial peptidoglycan (PG) sacculus that is covalently bound to an arabinogalactan (AG) layer (Alderwick et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge about cell wall structure supported by a citation.

claim: Mycolic acids form an outer membrane-like bilayer in Corynebacteria and Mycobacteria.
source: Mycolic acids are fused to the arabinose and form an outer membrane like bilayer, rendering the cell surface highly hydrophobic (Puech et al., 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: The mycolic acid membrane is an efficient barrier that protects cells from many conventional antibiotics.
source: The mycolic acid membrane (MM) is an efficient barrier that protects the cells from many conventional antibiotics.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the function of the mycolic acid membrane.

claim: Members of the Corynebacterianeae lack a mreB homologue and elongate apically.
source: In contrast to rod-shaped firmicutes and γ-proteobacteria, where cell-wall synthesis is dependent on the laterally acting MreB, members of the Corynebacterianeae lack a mreB homologue and elongate apically.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the growth mechanism of Corynebacterianeae.

claim: Apical elongation in C. glutamicum is mediated by the protein DivIVA.
source: This apical elongation is mediated by the protein DivIVA, which accumulates at the cell poles and serves as a scaffold for the organization of the elongasome complex (Letek et al., 2008; Hett and Rubin, 2008; Sieger et al., 2013; Figures 1 and 2A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and illustrated in Figures 1 and 2A,B.

claim: C. glutamicum lacks functional homologues of the Min- and nucleoid occlusion (Noc) system.
source: Without harboring any known functional homologues of the Min- and nucleoid occlusion (Noc) system, division typically results in unequally sized daughter cells (Donovan et al., 2013; Donovan and Bramkamp, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Division in C. glutamicum typically results in unequally sized daughter cells.
source: Without harboring any known functional homologues of the Min- and nucleoid occlusion (Noc) system, division typically results in unequally sized daughter cells (Donovan et al., 2013; Donovan and Bramkamp, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The spread in growth times between birth and division is much wider in C. glutamicum than in other model organisms.
source: Lastly, the spread in growth times between birth and division is much wider than in other model organisms, suggesting a weaker regulation of this growth feature (Donovan et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and suggests an inference about regulation.

claim: C. glutamicum exhibits a linear relationship between birth length and division length with a slope of 0.91±0.16.
source: For C. glutamicum, we find an approximately linear relationship between these birth and division lengths, with a slope of 0.91±0.16 (2xSEM, Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: C. glutamicum behaves close to the adder model on a population level.
source: This indicates that on a population level, C. glutamicum behaves close to the adder model, in which cells on average grow by adding a fixed length before dividing (Jun and Taheri-Araghi, 2015; Amir, 2014).
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data on birth and division lengths, supported by citations to theoretical frameworks.

claim: There is a systematic deviation from exponential growth in C. glutamicum when plotting ln(l_d/l_b) versus growth time.
source: By contrast, there appears to be a systematic deviation from this trend, with cells with shorter growth times lying above this line and cells with longer growth times lying below it, suggesting non-exponential elongation behavior.
evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: To distinguish between exponential and linear growth for an individual trajectory, the trajectory needs to be determined with an error of ~6%.
source: In fact, it has been estimated that to distinguish between exponential and linear growth for an individual trajectory, the trajectory needs to be determined with an error of ~6% (Cooper, 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The inferred average elongation rates have an error margin of around 8%.
source: Despite the high noise level of individual elongation trajectories, the inferred average elongation rates have an error margin of around 8%.
evidence: This is a result from the bootstrapping analysis of the inference method.

claim: Elongation rates of cells with larger birth length are consistently higher than the elongation rates of cells with smaller birth length.
source: Elongation rates of cells with larger birth length are consistently higher than the elongation rates of cells with smaller birth length.
evidence: This is an observation from the inferred elongation rate curves shown in Figure 5.

claim: The elongation rate curves initially increase, but then gradually level off toward a linear growth mode.
source: Strikingly, the elongation rate curves initially increase, but then gradually level off toward a linear growth mode (Figure 5).
evidence: This is the main finding from the elongation rate analysis, shown in Figure 5.

claim: There is a slight difference in cell elongation rates between the strain expressing DivIVA-mCherry and wild type cells.
source: We note a slight difference in the cell elongation rates between the strain expressing DivIVA-mCherry (Figure 5A) and wild type cells (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is an observation from comparing the data in Figures 5A and 5B.

claim: The difference in elongation rates between DivIVA-mCherry and wild type does not qualitatively change the mode of growth.
source: Importantly, this difference does not qualitatively change the mode of growth, but does show that a translational fusion to DivIVA tends to lower elongation rates.
evidence: This is an inference from comparing the growth modes in Figures 5A and 5B.

claim: The translational fusion to DivIVA tends to lower elongation rates.
source: Importantly, this difference does not qualitatively change the mode of growth, but does show that a translational fusion to DivIVA tends to lower elongation rates.
evidence: This is an inference from the observed difference in elongation rates.

claim: The lowered elongation rates in DivIVA-mCherry fusion likely reflect a disturbance in the interaction between RodA or bifunctional PBPs and the DivIVA-mCherry fusion protein.
source: This likely reflects a disturbance in the interaction between RodA or bifunctional PBPs and the DivIVA-mCherry fusion protein, indicating that the DivIVA-mCherry fusion is not fully functional.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed difference in elongation rates.

claim: The DivIVA-mCherry fusion is not fully functional.
source: This likely reflects a disturbance in the interaction between RodA or bifunctional PBPs and the DivIVA-mCherry fusion protein, indicating that the DivIVA-mCherry fusion is not fully functional. This is consistent with findings we reported earlier (Donovan et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Linear growth extends until the division time across division lengths in C. glutamicum.
source: Calculating the corresponding elongation rate curves, we find that that linear growth indeed extends until the division time across division lengths (inset Figure 5B,SI, Appendix 6—figure 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of elongation rates as a function of time until division.

claim: The onset of septum formation does not consistently coincide with the moment at which the elongation rate levels off.
source: We observe that the onset of septum formation does not consistently coincide with the moment at which the elongation rate levels off (Figure 5A): for smaller cells, the onset of septum formation occurs much later.
evidence: This is an observation from comparing septum formation timing with elongation rate curves in Figure 5A.

claim: It is implausible that the observed linear growth regime is due to the septum acting as a sink for cell-wall building blocks.
source: Therefore, it seems implausible that the observed linear growth regime is due the septum acting as a sink for cell-wall building blocks.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that septum formation timing does not coincide with the onset of linear growth.

claim: The rate of new cell wall formation is proportional to the number of TG sites in the RAG model.
source: To model this growth mechanism, we assume that the rate of new cell wall formation is proportional to the number of TG sites.
evidence: This is an assumption of the RAG model.

claim: The interaction between Lipid-II and TG sites can be described by Michaelis-Menten kinetics.
source: We describe the interaction between Lipid-II and TG sites by Michaelis-Menten kinetics (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a modeling assumption based on established biochemical kinetics.

claim: The polar HADA intensities are approximately proportional to the inferred average single-cell elongation rates.
source: Subsequently, we compute a moving average of the corrected polar HADA intensity as a function of cell length (Figure 6C). These polar HADA intensities are approximately proportional to the inferred average single-cell elongation rates (Appendix 8), as shown in the inset of Figure 6C.
evidence: This is a finding from the HADA staining experiment shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The polar HADA intensities are approximately proportional to the peptidoglycan insertion rate.
source: Thus, the polar HADA intensities can be used as a measure for the cellular elongation rate. Assuming a proportional relationship between elongation rate and peptidoglycan insertion rate, this implies the polar HADA intensities are also approximately proportional to the peptidoglycan insertion rate.
evidence: This is an inference from the observed proportionality between HADA intensity and elongation rate.

claim: Close to the cell tip, the HADA intensity remains approximately constant across cell lengths.
source: Analyzing the HADA intensity profile for smaller segments within the polar region, we find that the increase in intensity is unevenly distributed (Figure 6D). Close to the cell tip, the HADA intensity remains approximately constant across cell lengths, whereas a linear increase over cell lengths is seen further from the tip.
evidence: This is an observation from the HADA intensity analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Further from the cell tip, a linear increase in HADA intensity over cell lengths is observed.
source: Analyzing the HADA intensity profile for smaller segments within the polar region, we find that the increase in intensity is unevenly distributed (Figure 6D). Close to the cell tip, the HADA intensity remains approximately constant across cell lengths, whereas a linear increase over cell lengths is seen further from the tip.
evidence: This is an observation from the HADA intensity analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The predicted elongation rates from the RAG model provide a good fit to the experimental data for all studied genotypes.
source: The predicted elongation rates provide a good fit to the experiment for all studied genotypes (Figure 6E–G), although the data appear to exhibit a stronger inflection.
evidence: This is a finding from comparing model predictions to experimental data shown in Figures 6E-G.

claim: DivIVA recruits itself, leading to exponential growth of a nucleating DivIVA cluster.
source: There is evidence that transglycosylase RodA and PBPs are recruited to the cell pole via the curvature-sensing protein DivIVA (Letek et al., 2008; Sieger et al., 2013). As shown in Lenarcic et al., 2009, DivIVA also recruits itself, leading to the exponential growth of a nucleating DivIVA cluster.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The deletion of rodA results in a phenotype with a decreased population growth rate.
source: The SEDS-protein RodA is a mono-functional TG (Meeske et al., 2016; Emami et al., 2017; Sjodt et al., 2018), whose deletion results in a phenotype with a decreased population growth rate in the shaking-flask (Sieger et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The knockout of rodA is expected to lower the efficiency of polar cell wall formation.
source: We expect this knockout to lower the efficiency of polar cell wall formation, thus slowing down the rate-limiting step of growth.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the RAG model and the known function of RodA.

claim: The knockout of rodA mainly affects the efficiency of Lipid-II integration into the murein sacculus.
source: Specifically, we expect the knockout of rodA to mainly affect the efficiency of Lipid-II integration into the murein sacculus.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the known function of RodA.

claim: Elongation rate curves of the ΔrodA mutant are scaled down compared to wild type.
source: Indeed, we observe such a scaling down of the elongation rate curves (Figure 5C), lending further credence to our model for C. glutamicum growth.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 5C that validates the RAG model.

claim: The onset of linear growth regime occurs after approximately 20-25 minutes across growth conditions and birth lengths.
source: A striking feature observed across growth conditions and birth lengths, is the onset of a linear growth regime after approximately 20 min (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: This is an observation from the elongation rate curves shown in Figures 5A-C.

claim: The robustness of the timing of onset of linear growth can be understood from the RAG model.
source: The robustness of this timing can be understood from the RAG model: the regime of linear growth is reached via an exponential decay of the number of available TG sites until saturation is reached.
evidence: This is an explanation based on the mathematical properties of the RAG model.

claim: The degree of transglycosylase saturation at birth is comparable between wild-type and the ΔrodA mutant (~65% on average).
source: We find that this saturation is comparable between wild-type and the ΔrodA mutant (~65% on average), but significantly higher for DivIVA-labeled cells (~80% on average) (Appendix 9—tables 1 and 2).
evidence: This is a finding from fitting the RAG model to the experimental data.

claim: The degree of transglycosylase saturation at birth is significantly higher for DivIVA-labeled cells (~80% on average).
source: We find that this saturation is comparable between wild-type and the ΔrodA mutant (~65% on average), but significantly higher for DivIVA-labeled cells (~80% on average) (Appendix 9—tables 1 and 2).
evidence: This is a finding from fitting the RAG model to the experimental data.

claim: Asymmetric division and noise in individual growth times results in a dramatic widening of the cell-size distribution for a purely exponential grower.
source: It was shown that asymmetric division and noise in individual growth times results in a dramatic widening of the cell-size distribution for a purely exponential grower (Marantan and Amir, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous theoretical work.

claim: Single-cell variations have a much weaker impact on cell size distribution for an asymptotically linear grower than for an exponential grower.
source: For an asymptotically linear grower, however, we would expect single-cell variations to have a much weaker impact.
evidence: This is a prediction based on theoretical reasoning.

claim: The distribution of birth lengths for asymptotically linear growth closely matches the experimentally determined distribution.
source: The resulting distribution of birth lengths for the asymptotically linear growth case closely matches the experimentally determined distribution (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a finding from the simulation study shown in Figure 7.

claim: The distribution for exponential growth is much wider than the experimental distribution and exhibits a broad tail for longer cell lengths.
source: By contrast, the distribution for exponential growth is much wider, and exhibits a broad tail for longer cell lengths.
evidence: This is a finding from the simulation study shown in Figure 7.

claim: Linear growth can act as a regulator for cell size.
source: This indicates that linear growth can act as a regulator for cell size.
evidence: This is an inference from the simulation results showing narrower size distributions for linear growth.

claim: C. glutamicum has a high degree of variation of division symmetry.
source: C. glutamicum has a high degree of variation of division symmetry (Appendix 10—figure 1C) and single-cell growth times, but due to the asymptotically linear growth mode, the population-level variations in cell size are still relatively small.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Due to asymptotically linear growth mode, population-level variations in cell size are relatively small in C. glutamicum despite high variation in division symmetry and growth times.
source: C. glutamicum has a high degree of variation of division symmetry (Appendix 10—figure 1C) and single-cell growth times, but due to the asymptotically linear growth mode, the population-level variations in cell size are still relatively small.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the growth mode to population-level size variation.

claim: Apical cell wall formation is a plausible candidate for the rate-limiting step of growth in C. glutamicum.
source: For C. glutamicum, apical cell wall formation is a plausible candidate for the rate-limiting step of growth, because synthesis of the highly complex cell wall and lipids for the mycolic acid membrane is cost intensive and a major sink for energy and carbon in Corynebacteria and Mycobacteria (Brennan, 2003).
evidence: This is a speculation supported by a citation about the cost of cell wall synthesis.

claim: Synthesis of the highly complex cell wall and lipids for the mycolic acid membrane is cost intensive and a major sink for energy and carbon in Corynebacteria and Mycobacteria.
source: For C. glutamicum, apical cell wall formation is a plausible candidate for the rate-limiting step of growth, because synthesis of the highly complex cell wall and lipids for the mycolic acid membrane is cost intensive and a major sink for energy and carbon in Corynebacteria and Mycobacteria (Brennan, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: The binning method for analyzing elongation rates involves a tradeoff between bin width and error.
source: The binning method, however, involves a tradeoff: a smaller bin width results in a larger error on the inferred elongation rates, whereas a larger bin width averages out all variation within a larger birth length interval.
evidence: This is a methodological observation about the binning approach.

claim: The inference method developed in this study does not suffer from the binning-related tradeoff.
source: Our method does not suffer from this binning-related tradeoff, and it provides detailed elongation rate curves at any given birth length.
evidence: This is a claim about the advantages of the proposed method.

claim: Polar growth in Mycobacteria follows 'new end take off' (NETO) dynamics.
source: Polar growth was shown to follow 'new end take off' (NETO) dynamics (Hannebelle et al., 2020), in which the new cell pole makes a sudden transition from slow to fast growth, leading to a bilinear polar growth mode.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work on Mycobacteria.

claim: In C. glutamicum, the new pole gradually increases its average elongation rate before saturating to a constant maximum.
source: In our proposed growth model for C. glutamicum however, the new pole gradually increases its average elongation rate before saturating to a constant maximum.
evidence: This is a finding from the RAG model and experimental data.

claim: C. glutamicum deviates from NETO dynamics.
source: The deviation of C. glutamicum from NETO dynamics can also be seen by comparing each of the pole intensities in the HADA staining experiment, which does not show any signatures of NETO-like growth (Appendix 2—figure 11).
evidence: This is an observation from the HADA staining data.

claim: The asymptotically linear growth model accurately reproduces the experimental distribution of cell birth lengths.
source: We found that our asymptotically linear growth model accurately reproduces the experimental distribution of cell birth lengths.
evidence: This is a finding from the simulation study shown in Figure 7.

claim: A model of exponential growth predicts a much broader distribution of birth lengths with a long tail for larger birth lengths.
source: By contrast, a model of exponential growth predicts a much broader distribution with a long tail for larger birth lengths.
evidence: This is a finding from the simulation study shown in Figure 7.

claim: If single-cell growth variability is reduced by a factor 3, the distributions corresponding to both growth modes show a similarly narrow width.
source: Indeed, if single-cell growth variability is reduced by a factor 3, the distributions corresponding to both growth modes show a similarly narrow width (Appendix 10—figure 2).
evidence: This is a finding from additional simulations.

claim: An asymptotically linear grower is able to maintain a narrow distribution of cell sizes even for higher noise levels.
source: However, an asymptotically linear grower is able to maintain a narrow distribution of cell sizes even for higher noise levels, whereas for an exponential grower this distribution widens dramatically (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a finding from the simulation study shown in Figure 7.

claim: Most rod-shaped bacteria use sophisticated systems such as the Min system to ensure cytokinesis precisely at midcell.
source: Most rod-shaped bacteria use sophisticated systems, such as the Min system, to ensure cytokinesis precisely at midcell (Bramkamp et al., 2009; Lutkenhaus, 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Bacteria encoding a Min system grow by lateral cell wall insertion.
source: Bacteria encoding a Min system grow by lateral cell wall insertion.
evidence: This is established knowledge about bacterial growth mechanisms.

claim: Rod-shaped bacteria in the Actinobacteria phylum grow apically and do not contain a Min system.
source: In contrast, rod-shaped bacteria in the Actinobacteria phylum such as Mycobacterium or Corynebacterium species, grow apically and do not contain a Min system, nor any other known division site selection system (Donovan and Bramkamp, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: C. glutamicum couples division site selection to nucleoid positioning after chromosome segregation via the ParAB partitioning system.
source: C. glutamicum rather couples division site selection to nucleoid positioning after chromosome segregation via the ParAB partitioning system (Donovan et al., 2013), and has a broader distribution of division symmetries.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: Due to C. glutamicum's distinct growth mechanism, a more precise division site selection mechanism is not necessary to maintain a narrow cell size distribution.
source: We speculate that due to C. glutamicum's distinct growth mechanism, a more precise division site selection mechanism is not necessary to maintain a narrow cell size distribution.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the findings about linear growth and size distribution.

claim: The increase in cell mass is not necessarily proportional to cellular volume.
source: The elongation rates reported in this work reflect the increase in cellular volume over time. However, the increase in cell mass is not necessarily proportional to cellular volume.
evidence: This is a general statement about the relationship between mass and volume.

claim: In exponentially growing E. coli, cellular density systematically varies during the cell cycle.
source: In exponentially growing E. coli, the cellular density was recently reported to systematically vary during the cell cycle, while the surface-to-mass ratio was reported to remain constant (Oldewurtel et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to recent work on E. coli.

claim: The surface-to-mass ratio remains constant during the cell cycle in exponentially growing E. coli.
source: In exponentially growing E. coli, the cellular density was recently reported to systematically vary during the cell cycle, while the surface-to-mass ratio was reported to remain constant (Oldewurtel et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to recent work on E. coli.

claim: Mass production would follow exponential growth if mass production is proportional to protein content.
source: It is unknown how single-cell mass increases in C. glutamicum, but it would follow exponential growth if mass production is proportional to protein content.
evidence: This is a theoretical statement based on established principles.

claim: A regulatory mechanism for cell mass production that couples to cell volume is implied by the elongation rate curves obtained for the ΔrodA mutant.
source: The presence of a regulatory mechanism for cell mass production that couples to cell volume is implied by the elongation rate curves obtained for the ΔrodA mutant.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental observations on the ΔrodA mutant.

claim: Average mass production needs to be lowered in the ΔrodA mutant compared to WT to prevent cellular density from increasing indefinitely.
source: As the elongation rate is lower in this mutant, average mass production needs to be lowered compared to the WT in order to prevent the cellular density from increasing indefinitely.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the observation of lower elongation rates in the mutant.

claim: The growth trajectory inference method is not cell-type specific and can be used to obtain detailed growth dynamics in a wide range of organisms.
source: Our growth trajectory inference method is not cell-type specific, and can be used to obtain detailed growth dynamics in a wide range of organisms.
evidence: This is a claim about the generalizability of the method.

claim: The inferred asymptotically linear growth of C. glutamicum suggests the presence of novel growth regulatory mechanisms.
source: The inferred asymptotically linear growth of C. glutamicum deviates from the predominantly found exponential single-cell bacterial growth, and suggests the presence of novel growth regulatory mechanisms.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the findings of the study.

claim: Increases in cell length are proportional to increases in cell area in C. glutamicum.
source: Importantly, the increases in cell length are proportional to the increases in cell area (Appendix 2—figure 1A), suggesting that cellular length increase is also proportional to the volume increase.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Cellular length increase is proportional to volume increase in C. glutamicum.
source: Importantly, the increases in cell length are proportional to the increases in cell area (Appendix 2—figure 1A), suggesting that cellular length increase is also proportional to the volume increase.
evidence: This is an inference from the observed proportionality between length and area increases.

claim: C. glutamicum cells maintain a roughly constant cell width over the cell cycle.
source: This proportionality is expected since the rod-shaped C. glutamicum cells insert new cell wall material exclusively at the poles, while maintaining a roughly constant cell width over the cell cycle (Schubert et al., 2017; Daniel and Errington, 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: DivIVA localizes to the cell poles and to the newly formed division septum in C. glutamicum.
source: DivIVA is used as a marker for cell cycle progression, since it localizes to the cell poles and to the newly formed division septum in C. glutamicum (Letek et al., 2008; Donovan et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The Mother Machine is not ideally suited for C. glutamicum growth due to V-snapping at division.
source: The Mother Machine is not ideally suited for C. glutamicum growth, as the characteristic V-snapping at division could lead to shear forces and stress during cell separation, affecting growth (Zhou et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a methodological consideration supported by a citation.

claim: The mother machine has been shown to affect growth properties in some cells due to mechanical stresses inducing cell deformation.
source: Indeed, in some cases, the mother machine has been shown to affect growth properties even in cells not exhibiting V-snapping at division, due to mechanical stresses inducing cell deformation (Yang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: The sharp increase in average DivIVA-mCherry signal at the cell center is used as a proxy for the onset of septum formation.
source: To test this hypothesis, we used the moment of a sharp increase in the average DivIVA-mCherry signal at the cell center as a proxy for the moment of onset of septum formation (Appendix 2—figure 7): the inward growing septum introduces a negative curvature of the plasma membrane, leading to the accumulation of DivIVA (Lenarcic et al., 2009; Strahl and Hamoen, 2012).
evidence: This is a methodological approach supported by citations about DivIVA accumulation.

claim: The inward growing septum introduces a negative curvature of the plasma membrane, leading to the accumulation of DivIVA.
source: the inward growing septum introduces a negative curvature of the plasma membrane, leading to the accumulation of DivIVA (Lenarcic et al., 2009; Strahl and Hamoen, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: Lipid-II is translocated across the plasma membrane by the Lipid-II flippase MurJ.
source: At the TG sites, Lipid-II is translocated across the plasma membrane by the Lipid-II flippase MurJ (Sham et al., 2014; Kuk et al., 2017; Butler et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Transpeptidases conduct the crosslinking of peptide subunits, which contributes to the rigidity of the cell wall.
source: After PG building blocks provided by Lipid-II are incorporated into the existing cell wall by transglycolylation, transpeptidases (TP) conduct the crosslinking of peptide subunits, which contributes to the rigidity of the cell wall (Scheffers and Pinho, 2005; Valbuena et al., 2007; Schleifer and Kandler, 1972).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: RodA and bifunctional penicillin binding proteins (PBPs) are recruited by DivIVA.
source: During growth, the area of the PG sacculus, and thus the number of TG sites, is extended by RodA and bifunctional penicillin binding proteins (PBPs), recruited by DivIVA (Letek et al., 2008; Sieger et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: RodA is a mono-functional transglycosylase.
source: The SEDS-protein RodA is a mono-functional TG (Meeske et al., 2016; Emami et al., 2017; Sjodt et al., 2018)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Transglycosylase RodA and PBPs are recruited to the cell pole via the curvature-sensing protein DivIVA.
source: There is evidence that transglycosylase RodA and PBPs are recruited to the cell pole via the curvature-sensing protein DivIVA (Letek et al., 2008; Sieger et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: The inference method developed here can recover the input growth mode with high precision for linear, exponential, and the inferred growth modes.
source: We find that our inference method is able to recover the input growth mode with high precision in all cases (Appendix 4, Appendix 7), demonstrating the accuracy and internal consistency of our inference method.
evidence: This is a validation result from simulations testing the inference method.

claim: Faster-growing cells divide earlier than slower-growing cells for a given birth length.
source: For a given birth length, faster-growing cells divide earlier than slower-growing cells (Appendix 2—figure 2)
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Higher-order fitting functions result in negligible improvement of goodness-of-fit while increasing mean error on inferred elongation rates.
source: Higher-order fitting functions result in a negligible improvement of the goodness-of-fit, while increasing the mean error on inferred elongation rates (Appendix 2—figure 3).
evidence: This is a methodological finding from testing different fitting approaches.
